title: OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)

severity.usersAffected: ~3.6 million websites taken offline; ~30,000 servers destroyed
severity.impactUsd: Undetermined — total damages were still being assessed by a Strasbourg court-appointed expert panel at report time; no authoritative total was published

brief: In the early hours of 10 March 2021 a fire broke out in a ground-floor energy room at OVHcloud's SBG2 facility in Strasbourg, where the site's UPS units and their lead-acid battery banks were housed. Video surveillance and the fire panel traced the initiating event to a near-simultaneous electrical fault on UPS2 and its connected batteries. With no automatic suppression system in any of the five campus buildings, and a free-cooling design that used intumescent-treated raw-wood floors and single-skin cladding to aid airflow, the fire spread through the entire structure. De-energisation was slow because there was no accessible general site cut-off, forcing the grid operator to isolate an upstream substation; current was still present in the burning building well after the cut order. SBG2 was destroyed in its entirety, four of twelve rooms in adjacent SBG1 were partially destroyed, and the SBG2–SBG3 inter-building link was impacted. Roughly 30,000 servers were lost and about 3.6 million websites went offline. There were no casualties or injuries. French investigator BEA-RI could establish the fault location but not its precise cause, leaving several hypotheses open pending a court-expert examination.

magnitude.note: Extreme user and blast-radius impact — an entire data center destroyed with ~3.6M websites offline and ~30k servers lost, plus collateral damage to SBG1 and the SBG3 link. Financial score reflects a very large but formally unquantified loss (court-expert assessment still open). Duration score spans the ~9.5h fire fight and the multi-week service-restoration tail (recovery from 17 Mar; ~99% of key products re-delivered by 23 Apr).

sequenceOfEvents.event: Guard post receives a fire alarm originating in one of the SBG2 power (energy) rooms. Video surveillance and the fire control panel later show the initiating event was a near-simultaneous electrical fault on UPS2 and on the lead-acid batteries connected to it, housed in a separate room.
OVH calls the public fire service (SIS) to report the fire in the SBG2 energy room.
Order given to cut the site's power supply — but with no easily accessible general site cut-off device, isolation has to be performed at the upstream source substation.
Firefighters arrive on scene. Emergency services judge early that the free-cooling building design (raw-wood floors, single-skin/aluminium cladding) will not allow the fire to be contained.
OVH teams cut SBG2's building emergency energy.
OVH teams cut building emergency energy for SBG3, SBG1 and SBG4.
Grid operator Strasbourg Électricité Réseaux (SER) cut at the upstream source substation becomes effective.

Despite the substation cut, current is still present in SBG2 — now totally ablaze — and significant spread toward SBG1 is observed. The de-energisation delay blocks the massive early water deployment that could have contained the fire.
The EUROPA fireboat arrives to supply water by pumping from the Rhine canal, compensating for the single on-site hydrant's insufficient flow (<60 m3/h) and the absence of any OVH water reserve.
Site is fully de-energised — no more current anywhere on the site — enabling unrestricted water application.
Fire brought under control following full de-energisation and fireboat intervention.
Fire declared extinguished. SBG2 is destroyed in its entirety; SBG1 loses 4 of 12 rooms; the SBG2–SBG3 inter-building link is impacted. No casualties, no injuries.
Undamaged SBG3 and SBG4 data centers begin gradual restart, anchoring the recovery-side timeline.

OVH recovery status: Bare Metal ~99% re-delivered, Public Cloud Instance ~99% offered, VPS ~98% offered, Hosted Private Cloud ~88% restored on other sites; 8,000 services to be restored with their original IP by end of April; 150 SBG1 servers still to be reconnected. Croix factory output doubled from 1,500 to 3,000+ servers/week.

rootCause:
The BEA-RI official investigation (report N° MTE-BEARI-2022-005, French Ministry for the Ecological Transition) did NOT establish a confirmed ignition cause; the precise cause remained undetermined and under judicial expertise at the report's date. The fire originated in the "energy rooms" (salles énergie) of building SBG2 — the spaces housing the lead-acid battery banks and the uninterruptible power supplies (ASI/UPS) that back the servers — with fire starts appearing near-simultaneously (around 00:35) on batteries and on one UPS: "Les départs de feu se sont produits quasi-simultanément sur des batteries et sur un onduleur." Video-surveillance and the fire-panel monitoring localise an electrical fault to a specific UPS designated ASI2 in energy room no. 2 and to the batteries connected to it (which were in a separate room from the UPS). BEA-RI states plainly that the precise causes of these starts, subject to a judicial expertise, are not known as of the report and that it therefore does not position itself on this point: "Les causes précises des départs... qui font l'objet d'une expertise judiciaire, ne sont pas connues à la date du rapport."

The best-documented (but explicitly unconfirmed) hypothesis is an internal short-circuit provoked by liquid or humidity. ASI2 had recently been serviced for recurring, unexplained shifts into by-pass mode, yet the maintenance and return-to-service reports "ne mentionnent aucun élément singulier." Sensors on the rear of ASI2 recorded an anomalous hygrometry reading from around 23:15 on 9 March, rising again a little after 00:30. BEA-RI notes that "La présence d'un liquide ou d'humidité dans un appareil électrique peut causer la formation d'un court-circuit interne susceptible de causer les dégâts constatés," while cautioning "Cependant ces seuls éléments ne permettent toutefois pas de déterminer la cause de la défaillance." It leaves three hypotheses open — liquid/humidity linked to the nearby cooling system, a dysfunction connected to the maintenance done that same morning, or operation of the UPS outside its normal ranges — and does not choose between them. (The report also observes that OVH's lead-acid technology is comparatively robust and that internal short-circuits on it are rare.)

The safeguards that should have contained an incident in the energy rooms were absent by design. Those rooms had fire detection but no automatic extinguishing system, and OVH chose not to equip any of its five Strasbourg buildings with automatic fire protection ("OVH a choisi de n'équiper aucun des cinq bâtiments... de système de protection incendie automatique"). Battery health was not actively supervised: the 800 lead-acid batteries (30 kg, 13 kW each) had "aucun système de scrutation ou de supervision," OVH relying on the manufacturer's specified service life instead. Consequently a developing fault could progress to ignition with no automatic suppression and no continuous condition monitoring.

Once ignited, the SBG2 building accelerated rather than retarded propagation. SBG2 used OVH's modular free-cooling design over six levels on a steel frame (ossature acier), with raw wooden floors given an intumescent treatment ("planchers... en bois brut ayant subi un traitement intumescent") and large façade openings favouring thermal exchange with outside air. BEA-RI finds the chosen materials and the absence of floor overhang on the façade did not slow the fire, and that the building was highly permeable to outside air ("une grande perméabilité du bâtiment à l'air extérieur"): within the first 15 minutes, smoke detectors triggered at the ground floor and across all upper floors. The redundant power infrastructure obstructed the emergency response: there was no easily accessible general site cut-off (forcing the grid operator to cut supply at the source substation), and the backup generators auto-restarted despite the fire and had to be manually neutralised. The batteries were the last energy source, remaining live roughly twenty minutes after the general supply and generators were cut. The site was only electrically secured around 02:30 — the moment water attack could begin — by which time SBG2 was fully ablaze and spreading to adjacent buildings. Firefighting was further crippled by a single hydrant delivering below 60 m³/h and no operator water reserve, with the EUROPA fireboat proving decisive; fire doors held open during evacuation degraded the coupe-feu compartmentation between SBG2 and SBG3. The result was total destruction of SBG2 and partial destruction of SBG1 (4 of 12 rooms); per public sources cited in the report, roughly 3.6 million websites were unavailable at the peak.
contributingFactors: No automatic fire suppression anywhere on site: OVH deliberately chose not to equip any of its five Strasbourg buildings with automatic fire protection, and the energy rooms had detection but no automatic extinguishing system, so an incipient fire in the UPS/battery rooms could not be knocked down (or water deployed early, before power was cut) before it grew.

No battery condition monitoring: the 800 lead-acid batteries had no scrutation or supervision system; OVH relied solely on the manufacturer's specified service life, leaving no continuous means to detect a degrading or faulting unit before ignition.

Building design optimised for free-cooling worked against fire containment: six-level modular construction on a steel frame with raw wooden intumescent-treated floors, large façade air openings, and no floor overhang made SBG2 highly permeable to outside air, so smoke reached detectors on all floors within about 15 minutes.

Redundant power infrastructure obstructed the response: absence of an easily accessible general electrical cut-off (requiring the grid operator to cut at the source substation), plus backup generators that auto-restarted during the fire and had to be manually neutralised, and batteries that stayed live ~20 minutes after cut-off, delayed electrical securing of the site until ~02:30 — by which point SBG2 was fully ablaze.

Inadequate water resources: public responders had only a single hydrant delivering below 60 m³/h, and the operator held no dedicated extinguishing-water reserve nor pumping means from the Rhine canal, so large-scale firefighting could not begin promptly (the EUROPA fireboat, arriving ~03:00, was decisive).

Latent maintenance/humidity anomaly on ASI2: the UPS had recently been serviced for recurring, unexplained by-pass transitions, and anomalous hygrometry was recorded at its rear hours before ignition — an unresolved latent condition on the very unit implicated in the fire start, though BEA-RI could not confirm it as the cause.
Compartmentation lapse during evacuation: responders reported that coupe-feu doors were left open during evacuation, degrading the effectiveness of the 2-hour fire-wall separation protecting SBG3.

coe.action: Redefine the regulated unit as a 'charging workshop' — the room housing the batteries plus the charging equipment directly connected to them — so building fire-behaviour requirements cover the whole chain (protecting the battery storage room alone would not have prevented this fire).
In rebuilding and future data centers, incorporate SBG2 feedback into the design of buildings and energy (F/G) rooms, into detection and firefighting means, and into emergency procedures.

Establish and drill, through exercises, emergency procedures for securing electrical installations at the Strasbourg site to facilitate public emergency-service intervention (directly addressing the de-energisation delay).
Carry out a fleet-wide audit of all OVH facilities to study each site's vulnerability to fire risk.

Follow the battery manufacturer's guidance and set up monitoring of battery operating conditions and state to define preventive-maintenance/replacement rules; where battery counts are large, deploy BMS/polling data-management (VII.5).

Size operators and local emergency services to cope with a widespread-fire scenario, treating it as a plausible case; meet ICPE water-resource requirements (VII.6 — initial requirements were found unmet).

Rather than classifying data centers under the Environment Code (ICPE), adopt the profession's/insurers' professional fire-safety guides and have ANSSI incorporate those security recommendations into its certification (VII.7).

lessonsLearnt: Fire detection without automatic suppression buys almost no containment time in a data center — SBG2 rooms had detection but no extinguishing system, and water could not be applied early without first cutting power.

The battery-charging chain, not just the battery room, is the true hazard unit; the UPS and its batteries were in separate rooms and the fault spanned both, so single-room protection would not have prevented the fire.

Energy-efficient free-cooling construction (combustible raw-wood floors, single-skin cladding) trades fire compartmentation for airflow — the same design that cuts cooling energy accelerated vertical fire spread.
A facility must be de-energisable quickly and locally; relying on an upstream substation cut left the building live for over an hour, blocking safe massive water application while the fire grew.

On-site water resilience matters — a single hydrant below 60 m3/h with no reserve and no canal-pumping capability forced dependence on an external fireboat that arrived roughly two hours into the incident.
Preventive battery monitoring (operating conditions and state, per manufacturer rules, with BMS at scale) is essential observability; the exact fault cause could not be determined afterward.
A total-loss fire is a plausible, not far-fetched, scenario for a data center and must be planned for by both operators and local emergency services.
improvements: Rebuild energy rooms and buildings with automatic fire suppression and proper fire-behaviour construction, incorporating SBG2 feedback into detection, firefighting means, and emergency procedures.
Install an easily accessible general site cut-off and drill electrical-securing procedures so responders can safely deploy water within minutes rather than hours.
Provide on-site extinguishing-water reserves and/or canal-pumping capability sized for a widespread-fire scenario, and ensure ICPE water-resource requirements are met.
Treat the whole charging workshop (batteries plus charging equipment) as the regulated fire unit and design its compartmentation accordingly.
Deploy battery monitoring / BMS with manufacturer-based preventive-maintenance and replacement rules across large battery fleets.
Run a fleet-wide fire-vulnerability audit of all facilities and feed findings into rebuild standards.

Advance professional fire-safety guides and ANSSI certification for data centers instead of ICPE classification, reflecting that the dominant consequence is economic/strategic (data loss and service unavailability) rather than human or environmental.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Failure mechanism: an undetermined fault in the power backbone
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The incident began not in the IT halls but in SBG2's power backbone. Surveillance and the fire panel place the initiating electrical fault on UPS2 and its associated lead-acid battery bank, with outbreaks appearing almost simultaneously on batteries and an inverter located in a separate room. Crucially, BEA-RI could not establish why the UPS failed, floating three hypotheses — liquid or humidity from the adjacent cooling system, a fault tied to a maintenance operation performed that same morning, or operation of the inverter outside normal ranges. The use of lead-acid rather than lithium chemistry, which BEA-RI regards as robust and rarely subject to internal short circuits, makes the ignition all the more anomalous and is why the precise mechanism was handed to a court-appointed expert.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Why it cascaded: a design optimised against containment
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Several deliberate design choices converted a localised electrical fault into a total loss. No automatic suppression existed in any of the five buildings, so water could not be applied until power was cut. The free-cooling architecture — intumescent-treated raw-wood floors and single-skin/aluminium cladding chosen to maximise heat exchange and minimise cooling energy — offered combustible pathways and little compartmentation, and responders judged on arrival that it would not permit containment. Compounding this, there was no accessible general cut-off: de-energisation had to wait for an upstream substation isolation, and current was still present in the fully-ablaze building at 02:14, more than an hour after the 00:58 cut order. Each efficiency- or cost-driven decision individually plausible combined into a system with no early line of defence.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Recovery: external water, mass replacement, and cross-site failover
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: With one hydrant under 60 m3/h and no on-site reserve or canal-pumping capability, effective firefighting depended on the EUROPA fireboat, which arrived around 02:57, and on full de-energisation at 03:28; the fire was controlled by 06:45 and extinguished by 10:02, with the intervention closed at 18:13 and no casualties. Service recovery leaned on the surviving campus and OVH's manufacturing: SBG3 and SBG4 restarted from 17 March, the Croix factory doubled output from 1,500 to over 3,000 servers per week, and by 23 April Bare Metal, Public Cloud and VPS were roughly 98–99% re-delivered while Hosted Private Cloud reached 88% on other sites, with 8,000 services slated to return on their original IPs. Customers who suffered permanent data loss, however, could not be made whole by capacity alone.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Organisational and systemic factors
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The investigation frames the loss less as a freak accident than as an accumulation of risk-acceptance decisions: choosing no suppression across the whole campus, building for cooling efficiency over fire compartmentation, and not meeting the initial ICPE water-resource requirements. BEA-RI's remedies are structural — redefine the regulated 'charging workshop' to cover batteries plus charging equipment, drill electrical-securing procedures, audit the entire fleet for fire vulnerability, and monitor battery state proactively. Notably, BEA-RI concluded data centers should not be ICPE-classified, arguing the dominant consequence of such a fire is economic and strategic (data loss and service unavailability) rather than human or environmental, and pointing instead to professional fire-safety guides and ANSSI certification.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Cross-incident pattern: single-facility concentration and thin defence-in-depth
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: SBG2 is a canonical example of correlated failure: tens of thousands of servers and millions of dependent websites concentrated in one building whose defensive layers — suppression, compartmentation, rapid de-energisation, and water supply — were all thin or absent simultaneously, so a single power-room fault removed everything at once. The recurring lesson mirrors other large outages: efficiency and cost optimisations that quietly erode independent safety layers, plus customer over-reliance on a single site without geo-redundant backups, turn a contained component fault into a headline loss. Resilience here was ultimately proven not by the facility's own defences but by cross-site failover and industrial replacement capacity.

technicalDeepDive:
The initiating event was an electrical fault localised via video-surveillance and fire-panel monitoring to UPS unit ASI2 in energy room no. 2 and to its associated battery bank (housed in a separate room), with fire starts appearing near-simultaneously (~00:35) on the batteries and on the UPS. BEA-RI did not establish the cause and did not position itself on it, the matter being under judicial expertise. The best-documented but unconfirmed mechanism is an internal short-circuit provoked by liquid or humidity ingress: the report records anomalous hygrometry at the rear of ASI2 from around 23:15 on 9 March, rising again a little after 00:30, and notes that moisture inside an electrical device can create an internal short-circuit capable of causing the observed damage — while stressing these elements alone do not allow the cause to be determined. It ties a plausible humidity source to the cooling system located nearby. Two further hypotheses remain open: a dysfunction connected to the maintenance performed on ASI2 that same morning (it had been serviced for recurrent, unexplained by-pass transitions, though the reports flagged nothing singular), or operation of the UPS outside its normal ranges. Notably, BEA-RI adds that OVH's lead-acid technology is more robust and stable than lithium and that internal short-circuits on it are rare — a caveat against over-weighting the short-circuit hypothesis.

Physically, a UPS energy room concentrates high stored electrical energy: 800 lead-acid batteries of 30 kg rated 13 kW each. With no automatic extinguishing system in the energy rooms and no battery supervision to flag a degrading unit, a fault could escalate to open flame unchecked. The near-simultaneous starts on both ASI2 and its connected batteries (in a separate room) are consistent with a fault propagating along the DC link between the UPS and its battery string, though the report does not assert the propagation path and OVH could not supply the UPS operating parameters (voltage, current, mode) at the moment of failure.

Escalation was governed by the building envelope and the power topology. The free-cooling design — raw wooden intumescent-treated floors, steel frame, large façade openings, no façade floor overhang — made the building highly permeable to outside air, so smoke reached detectors across all six levels within 15 minutes; the first floor was fully involved by ~01:28 and second-floor temperature sensors saturated by ~01:40. Crucially, the fire could not be safely fought while live: backup generators auto-restarted despite the fire and had to be neutralised, there was no easily accessible general cut-off (the grid operator had to cut at the source substation, effective ~01:50), and the batteries remained an energy source for about 20 minutes after the general supply and generators were cut. Electrical securing was therefore only achieved around 02:30 — also when large-scale water attack began — by which time SBG2 was fully engulfed. BEA-RI's retrospective judgement is that protecting the battery room alone would not have prevented the fire, because the near-simultaneous start in the onduleur room (not explicitly covered by ICPE atelier-de-charge rules) also occurred; fire-behaviour requirements therefore need to apply to all rooms housing the electrical equipment that charges and is directly connected to the batteries.
